column9: The interior of the snow-block magnetic observatory built on the floe beside HMS Alert at Floeberg Beach: the unifilar magnetometer on its stone pillar, an observer sitting on a block reading his notebook by candle, a dog curled on the floor, and the vaulted snow roof with its blocks laid in courses. It is one of very few pictures of a British polar magnetic observatory in use.

Five of the Alert's people cutting and laying snow blocks to build the row of snow houses that Moss calls the snow town, with a lantern on the snow, a shovel, a finished dome behind and the ship's masts on the horizon. Moss's text notes how a spirit spill made one house smell ever after like a gin-palace, another of oysters, and that inside them the snow transmitted a subdued greenish-blue light, such as a diver sees deep under water.

column5: Effect of Extreme Cold on a Candle
column9: A candle whose flame has sunk into a tallow net-work cylinder, the wax standing up in a lace of ribs around it. Moss offers it as a demonstration of the still air and low temperature inside a snow house.

Two men in furs at the open door of one of the snow-banked buildings on the floe, a third going away to the right, an alpenstock leaning by the door. Moss's facing text describes carrying no arms because they were beyond the region of the sea bear, the point marked by four barrels supporting a flagstaff, and a temperature of 67 degrees below freezing that was perfectly calm and not too cold to rest a moment or two in.

Seven men of a sledge crew inside their tent at the end of a march, three already in the sleeping bag, one sitting up smoking, the rolled robes and the frozen blanket wrappers around them. Moss describes the officer sleeping as the outside man at the end of the tent away from the door, whose duty is to call the cook, and the cook lighting his lamp, melting snow and scraping down cocoa before walking in over his sleeping companions and brushing the festoons of frozen breath off the tent. Position is the sledging ground north of Floeberg Beach.

Two men with alpenstocks standing at the lip of a crevasse in a great snow bank near Cape Joseph Henry, with the pyramid of a pressed-up floe beyond. Moss calls the bank a miniature discharging glacier, the only one met with on that coast, and records that it was strong enough to carry the heavily laden sledges of the western parties.

A low shelter of stones on a gravel beach, built by Inuit hunters as a blind for taking birds, drawn by Moss on the coast of Robeson Channel during the ships' retreat south. It is a hunting structure, not a dwelling, and one of the northernmost recorded on the Ellesmere coast. Position approximate.

Allman Bay on the Ellesmere coast, its head ringed with snow-streaked hills, drawn as the ships came south in September 1876. The bay is named after Professor George James Allman; Moss's text on the same page records the ships pushing through thin floe towards the water spaces near Norman Lockyer Island, the Discovery leading because the shape of her bow let her glide up on the ice until her weight broke it down.
